newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - To stay firm, if gas oil does.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - To stay firm, if gas oil does.

text.p: European crudes are likely to stay firm into this week if gas oil maintains its five-year refining margins and lifts the rest of the barrel with it, dealers said.
"As long as there is strong support for gas oil, the market for crude will remain strong," a North Sea trader said.
All eyes will be on gas oil-rich grades like Oseberg and Forties, both of which are virtually sold in the second decade and scarce in the third, despite sharply higher premiums.
Oseberg, which yields roughly 40 percent gas oil, was valued at 50 cents over Dated Brent on Friday.
Forties, in demand for its high quality gas oil, was also trading at up to a 40-cent premium to physical Brent.
Brent remains the sick man of the physical market, struggling all last week to achieve a premium over November paper but rising on lack of availability of other North Sea grades, traders said.
Offers on short-term CFD swaps for this week rose to November +13 cents.
Traders said the Brent loading programme for the last decade was roughly equal to the first, with 14 cargoes loading during the period.
They said that at current levels of just 10 cents over November paper, Brent should start to see some interest and rise in line with the other North Sea grades of comparable quality such as Forties.

The fate of Brent was likely to be determined by a trader now holding seven cargoes of Brent destined for the U.S. Gulf and South Africa. Any change in plan and the reappearance of prompt Brent cargoes on the market could depress prices further.
"Either other grades have to come down or Brent has to go up, and it looks like the latter at the moment," said a trader.
Gasoline-rich Ekofisk was likely to remain depressed with a number of cargoes before the end of the month still to find homes.

Sour Flotta weakened in line with lower numbers seen for Mediterranean sour marker Russian Urals, which has come off in the last few days on ample availability and the reopening of the port of Novorossiisk after pipeline maintenance.

The main determinant of crude values has been strength in gas oil, with distillate grades benefiting as refinery margins rose in line with the expanding crack spread, which stood at around $8 a barrel on Friday afternoon.

With heating oil stocks still low on both sides of the Atlantic, refiners saw continued good demand for gas oil grades in NWE and the Med, with refiners in the two regions seen absorbing West African grades which were unlikely to move into the Asian market, given the ballooning Brent/Dubai arbitrage.
The Brent/WTI arbitrage window was also unworkable, and one wet trader said a few earlier Brent cargoes were still looking for homes in the U.S. Gulf.
"For the time being, demand in Europe and the Med are good enough," a trader for a U.K. major said.
